paragraph: Khara was outraged at the sight of Surpanakha as she lay at his feet, with her disfigured face. "Rise", he said, "and tell me the reason for this atrocity. Who has dared to provoke a venomous snake without cause? Who in his ignorance tries to put around his neck the noose of death? Consider him already dead. Strong, powerful, able to assume any form at will and mighty as Yama that you are, who has caused you this disfigurement? Struck by my arrows, whose blood shall bathe this earth and on whose flesh will the vultures feed in delight? Neither the devatas, pisachas ghandarvas nor the rakshasas can save him." Surpanakha told Khara of what had happened. "Two men, young and handsome have arrived in Dandaka. They have beautiful eyes like the petals of the white lotus. Wearing deerskin and matted hair they live the simple life of ascetics, subsisting on forest fare. They are Rama and Lakshmana sons of Dasaratha. Handsome as Gandharvas, they bear all signs of royalty, but I do not know whether they are men or gods. With them is a woman, slender of waist, young, beautiful and bejeweled. It is because of her that I have been reduced to this plight. I crave to drink the blood of Rama and Lakshmana, as they lie dead on the battlefield and the blood of that wretched woman! Dear brother will you help me to fulfill my wish?" Khara summoned fourteen of the fiercest rakshasas, each equal to the might of the Lord of Death. To them he commanded, "Armed, wearing bark and skin, two mortals, accompanied by a woman, have entered Dandaka. Kill them and bring their bodies. My sister desires to drink their blood". The demons rose and left like ominous rain clouds, unaware that Rama's sharp, unerring arrows would soon kill them all.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Surpanakha, disfigured by Lakshmana, recounts her humiliation to her brother Khara, exaggerating the slight and focusing on her desire for revenge against Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita. Enraged and protective of his sister's honor, Khara immediately dispatches fourteen powerful Rakshasas to kill Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita and bring their bodies back for Surpanakha to drink their blood, setting up a direct confrontation.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage highlights the dangers of uncontrolled anger, inflated ego, and the pursuit of vengeance. Khara's immediate and disproportionate response to Surpanakha's disfigurement, without fully understanding the circumstances, demonstrates his rash and violent nature. Surpanakha's continued vengeful desires, even after being punished, show her unrepentant evil. The command to kill innocent individuals for personal vendetta exemplifies adharma and foreshadows the inevitable consequences of such actions when confronted by righteous power.
Outcome/Resolution: Khara, fueled by rage and his sister's desire for revenge, sends fourteen powerful Rakshasas to kill Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita. This act directly escalates the conflict between the Rakshasas and Rama, setting the stage for a violent confrontation where the Rakshasas are ultimately unaware of the divine power they are about to face.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Krodha (Rage/Anger - Khara's overwhelming anger, Surpanakha's continued anger)
Ahankara (Ego/Pride - Khara's boastful pronouncements of power, his defense of his sister's 'honor')
Pratishodh (Vengeance - Surpanakha's desire for revenge, Khara's immediate action)
Moha (Delusion/Ignorance - The Rakshasas' unawareness of Rama's true power, leading them to their doom)
Adharma (Unrighteousness - The act of attacking ascetics and innocent individuals for revenge)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Spiritually, this passage highlights the destructive cycle of Krodha (anger) and Pratishodh (vengeance) driven by Ahankara (ego), especially when coupled with Moha (delusion). Khara's outrage at Surpanakha's disfigurement, fueled by his immense ego and pride in his power, leads him to immediately resort to extreme violence without proper discernment. Surpanakha's continued desire to 'drink the blood' of her perceived tormentors underscores her deeply rooted Adharmic nature. The Rakshasas, blinded by their delusion and loyalty to their enraged leader, are depicted as 'ominous rain clouds' heading towards their inevitable demise, spiritually illustrating the ultimate futility and self-destruction inherent in acting from unrighteous impulses against divine order.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, this scene is dominated by Khara's intense and uncontrolled anger management issues. The sight of Surpanakha's disfigurement instantly triggers a violent outburst, showcasing a complete lack of emotional regulation and an overwhelming ego that makes him feel untouchable and entitled to mete out death. Surpanakha's continued focus on drinking the blood of her adversaries demonstrates a deep-seated desire for vengeance, stemming from her humiliation. The immediate deployment of his forces, without any rational inquiry, portrays a mind consumed by rage and pride, leading to a rash decision that foreshadows a significant psychological confrontation for the Rakshasas, whose overconfidence will lead to their ultimate undoing.
